easy.heading: Starting My Morning With A Quick Win
easy.body:
Solving the easy puzzle today was all about finding those single-cell sum targets first. I noticed right away that cells (3,0) and (3,2) both had a sum target of zero. This is a huge hint because it means those spots have to be a blank side of a domino. I also saw that cell (4,0) needed to be a 5 and cell (2,1) needed to be a 2. Filling these in first gave me a great head start and made the grid feel much less empty.

Next, I looked at the equals constraints. Since I knew (3,0) was a 0 and it was part of the [0,0] domino connecting it to (2,0), that meant (2,0) was also a 0. Because cell (1,0) had to equal (2,0), I knew (1,0) had to be a 0 as well. This led me to place the [4,0] domino vertically at the top left. Following these logical links is my favorite part of the game because it feels like a chain reaction where one move solves the next.

To finish up, I focused on the bottom right corner. Cell (4,2) had to equal (4,1). Since (3,2) was a 0 and part of the [1,0] domino, (4,2) became a 1. To satisfy the rule, (4,1) had to be a 1 as well. This left me with the [5,1] domino for the bottom left. It was a really smooth solve that only took a few minutes once those first few numbers were in place.

medium.heading: Stepping Up The Game For Medium Mode
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today was a bit more of a brain teaser, especially with that less than constraint. I started with cell (1,0), which was a single-cell sum target of 3. It was part of a domino with (1,1), and since (1,1) had to match (2,1) and (2,1) had to match (2,2), I had a little path of equal values to figure out. I used the [2,2] domino across the top for (0,1) and (0,2), which helped me realize that the middle values needed to be a bit higher to satisfy the other sums.

I hit a small snag on the right side of the board. The sum target for (0,4) and (0,5) was 3, and I also had a separate target of 3 for the single cell at (1,5). By placing the [3,0] end of a domino at (1,5) and (0,5), I was able to meet both rules perfectly. This left (0,4) open to pair with (0,3) using the [4,3] domino. It's all about checking which numbers are left in your tray and seeing where they fit into the remaining puzzles.

The final piece of the puzzle was the less than box at the bottom right. The target was 4 for the sum of cells (2,4) and (2,5). I looked at my last few tiles and the [2,1] domino was the perfect fit. Since 2 plus 1 is 3, and 3 is less than 4, it satisfied the constraint perfectly. It always feels so good when the last domino fits exactly where it's supposed to go without any leftover pieces.

hard.heading: A Real Brain Buster For The Hard Grid
hard.body:
Wow, today's hard puzzle really pushed me! The biggest challenge was the huge sum target of 12 for cells (0,4) and (1,4). In a game of dominoes, the only way to get a 12 is to have two 6s. I looked at my list and saw the [1,6] and [0,6] dominoes. I had to arrange them so the 6s landed in those specific sum cells. It took a few tries to get the orientation right so I didn't block the equals constraint at (0,3) and (1,3).

Another tricky area was the long sum at the very bottom. Cells (4,1), (4,2), (4,3), and (4,4) had to add up to exactly 4. That is very difficult when you have four different cells to fill! I realized I had to use a lot of 0s and 1s there. This forced me to use the [1,1] and [4,2] dominoes in a very specific way to keep the total low. Once those low-value tiles were placed, the rest of the board started to make a lot more sense.

The breakthrough happened when I tackled the middle section where (2,3), (3,2), and (3,3) all had to be equal. I found that using a 3 in those spots worked with the remaining [3,3] and [3,5] dominoes. Connecting that middle section to the bottom sum of 11 for cells (3,0) and (3,1) was the final hurdle. It was like finishing a very complex machine where every gear finally clicked into place. If you're struggling with this one, my advice is to focus on that bottom sum of 4 first!

explanation.tips: Try to find the single-cell sum targets first because they give you a guaranteed number to work with. Look for very large sums like 11 or 12 or very small sums like 0 or 1, as these have fewer combinations of dominoes that can fit. If you get stuck, look at the equals constraints to see if they create a chain of the same number across the grid.
explanation.learned: I learned that when a puzzle has a long row of cells that must sum to a small number, it really limits your options and forces you to save your blank and 1-pip dominoes for that area. It was also interesting to see how a sum target of zero is essentially a free gift that helps you place blank dominoes right away.

faqs.question: How do I solve sum constraints in Pips?
faqs.answer: Sum constraints are shown in outlined regions with a number in the corner. All the pips on the dominoes placed in that region must add up to that total number.

faqs.question: What does the equals sign mean in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: The equals sign means that every cell inside that specific region must have the same number of pips, regardless of which domino they belong to.

faqs.question: Are blank domino sides worth zero points?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the Pips puzzle, the blank side of a domino counts as zero when calculating sums for the target regions.

faqs.question: Can you use the same domino twice in one puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, you are given a specific set of dominoes for each puzzle, and each one can only be placed on the grid once.

faqs.question: How does the less than target work?
faqs.answer: A less than constraint means the sum of the pips in that region must be smaller than the number shown in the target box.

faqs.question: What is the best way to start a Hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Start by identifying the most restrictive regions, such as very high sums or very low sums, and use the process of elimination with your available dominoes.
